summary: Describes an optional IS-IS mechanism for running several independent IP topologies inside a single IS-IS domain. It can be used for things like a separate management network over the original one. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS normally calculates routes for one topology. This RFC lets routers keep several separate topology views within one IS-IS domain, with a separate route calculation for each.

subtitle: How one IS-IS domain can advertise and compute routes for several separate IP topologies.

tldr.problem: A standard IS-IS domain computes one topology, but operators may need separate routes for management, IPv6, multicast or selected address spaces.
tldr.mechanism: Routers mark adjacencies, reachable systems and prefixes with Multi-Topology IDs carried in new TLVs. Each topology runs its own shortest-path computation.
tldr.outcome: A single IS-IS domain can carry independent IP topologies. MT ID 0 remains the standard topology, and routers without the extension can continue to use it.

today: RFC 5120 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Run Multiple Topologies
sections.content:
RFC 5120 defines an optional Multi-Topology (MT) extension for IS-IS. It lets one IS-IS domain maintain several independent IP topologies instead of applying the same routes to every traffic type.

The RFC gives examples including an in-band management network, separate IPv6 or multicast routing, and directing a subset of addresses along a different topology. The ordinary IS-IS topology is identified as MT ID 0.

The extension adds information for adjacency formation, reachable systems and prefixes, and uses that information in a topology-specific shortest-path-first computation.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators may need different routes for management, IPv6, multicast or selected destinations. The extension lets IS-IS calculate those routes separately within the same domain.

sections.title: Forming Adjacencies
sections.content:
Each adjacency belongs to a set of topologies on its interface. A new TLV in IS-IS Hello packets advertises that set. If the TLV is absent, the interface is treated as supporting MT ID 0 only.

On a point-to-point interface, a router must not advertise a neighbor in a topology that the neighbor did not include in its hello. Routers should not form an adjacency when they have no common topology.

On a LAN, routers always form adjacencies even without a common MT. This allows all routers to elect the same Designated Intermediate System. The pseudo-node LSP remains unchanged and lists all LAN nodes regardless of their MT support.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers advertise which topologies they support on each interface. Point-to-point neighbors use only shared topologies, while LAN routers still form adjacencies so they can elect one designated system.

sections.title: The Four Topology TLVs
sections.content:
RFC 5120 defines four TLVs. The Multi-Topology TLV, type 229, lists the MT IDs a router or interface supports. Each entry is two bytes and contains a 12-bit MT ID, an overload bit, an attach bit and reserved bits. One TLV can advertise up to 127 topologies.

The MT Intermediate Systems TLV, type 222, advertises neighbor reachability. The MT Reachable IPv4 Prefixes TLV, type 235, and MT Reachable IPv6 Prefixes TLV, type 237, advertise prefixes. Each carries its MT membership along with reachability information in the corresponding existing format.

The reachability TLVs for intermediate systems and IPv4 prefixes must be ignored when their MT ID is zero. The ordinary IS-IS reachability information represents the standard topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Four new TLV types identify topology membership, neighbor reachability and IPv4 or IPv6 prefixes. Their MT IDs tell receiving routers which topology each item belongs to.

sections.title: Separate Shortest-Path Calculations
sections.content:
Each topology must run its own routing decision process. The pseudo-node LSPs are shared during calculations, but the reverse-connectivity check and next hops must stay within the same MT.

The RFC recommends keeping each topology's results in a separate Routing Information Base (RIB). Overlapping addresses in different topologies can otherwise produce undesirable routes, including forwarding loops. One topology cannot use another topology's information inside its SPF calculation.

Route leaking between IS-IS levels should occur only within the same MT. Overload, partition and attached status in the main LSP header describe the default topology; non-default topologies carry their own overload and attach bits in the MT TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Each topology calculates its own shortest paths and should keep its results separate. Routers must use next hops from the same topology as the routes they computed.

sections.title: Topology IDs and Forwarding
sections.content:
MT IDs are 12 bits. ID 0 is the standard topology; IDs 1 through 5 are reserved for IPv4 management, IPv6 routing, IPv4 multicast, IPv6 multicast and IPv6 management. IDs 6 to 3995 are reserved for IETF consensus, and 3996 to 4095 are for development, experimental and proprietary uses.

When multiple topologies use the same address family, a router must determine which routing table an incoming packet belongs to. Separate interfaces or non-overlapping address ranges can identify the topology. If addresses overlap on a shared interface, an additional local policy is needed; that mechanism is outside the RFC's scope.

A management topology can include all routers even when ordinary traffic does not use it. Alternatively, an operator may extend the default topology to management-only nodes and assign high link costs so ordinary data traffic avoids those links.
sections.plainLanguage: The MT ID identifies a topology, but forwarding still needs a way to select the right routing table. The RFC describes options and leaves selection policy to each network.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says no specific new security issue is known. IS-IS authentication applies to all protocol data units regardless of whether they carry MT information. If changing topology information is a high risk, the RFC recommends applying an authentication mechanism such as RFC 3567.

When topologies share an interface and address space, a misconfiguration or spoofed source address can send packets through the wrong routing table. This may cause packet loss or unauthorized use of network resources.

IANA registered TLV types 222, 229, 235 and 237 and created the IS-IS Multi-Topology Parameters registry. IDs 6 to 3995 use Expert Review; IDs 3996 to 4095 are for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication can protect topology information in IS-IS messages. Networks also need to ensure that packets are assigned to the intended topology when several share an interface.
